How Do I Talk to My Teenage Son About Social Media and Dating?

May 17, 2026, 20:00 IST

These conversations can feel intimidating, especially because it is hard to know where to begin or how much to say. The good news is that it does not have to be one big, serious talk. In fact, it usually works better as an ongoing conversation that evolves over time, where your son feels safe asking questions and sharing his thoughts without fear of being judged or shut down.

Avoid starting from where you think the right place is, as that may result in a conversation that feels awkward, forced or clunky, and your son may feel uncomfortable and try to tune you out. Instead, find a way to understand what he already knows or what he currently wonders about the world of sex and relationships, and establish yourself as a calm and non-judgemental adult who he can turn to for helpful advice rather than turn to friends with no life experience or strangers online who may not offer the right advice for him.

When it comes to relationships, what matters most is helping him understand respect, consent, emotional responsibility, and communication. This includes recognising boundaries, handling rejection, and understanding that relationships are not just about attraction but also about how you treat another person. With social media, it becomes important to talk about how online spaces can distort expectations around bodies, relationships, and attention, and how validation through likes or messages does not always reflect real connection. He also needs to be able to think deeply about safety on digital spaces both for himself and for the people he speaks with, and this requires you to be up-to-date on how younger generations use the internet to socialise and build deep connections too. Do not be afraid to reach out to therapists, adolescent behavioural specialists and sex educators who may be able to guide you on what to expect when it comes to teenagers and their rapidly evolving relationships with the internet.

You do not need to have perfect answers. Being open, honest, and willing to listen goes a long way. It can also help to share your own values and perspectives in a way that feels relatable rather than instructional, so that the conversation feels like guidance rather than a lecture. Do not be embarrassed to admit when you do not have an answer to something, and reassure him that you would like to look into his area of concern and come back to him once you find an answer. What he needs is a safe adult who gives him room to explore himself, have new experiences, be confused with, be scared with, receive helpful advice and validation from, while also being able to make mistakes and develop an instinct for taking accountability and repairing from any harm he may cause. What you are building is trust, so that he knows he can come to you as he navigates these experiences. But it is so much more. It is an environment that fosters his individuality and humanity, where he can be both vulnerable and responsible, and these conversations will form the foundation for how he sees the world and himself for years to come.

You may make mistakes of your own, and it is important to take responsibility and commit to repairing the space when you do, as your son is not only learning from your advice but learning by emulating you too. Let him see that mistakes are normal, and that growing into an adult is not about perfection without mistakes but about repairing and learning with grace.

This is often where people start to worry that something is wrong, but a drop in sexual desire can happen for many reasons that have little to do with love itself. Stress, mental load, hormonal shifts, routine, body image, or even the predictability of long-term relationships can all influence desire in subtle ways.

It can help to move away from the idea of fixing desire quickly and instead get curious about what has changed for you. Desire is not always spontaneous. For many people, it becomes more responsive over time, meaning it shows up after arousal begins rather than before. This means that waiting to feel in the mood before engaging may keep you stuck in a loop of disinterest. At the same time, you should not feel pressured to say yes when you genuinely don’t want to.

Opening a conversation with your husband about how you’ve been feeling, without framing it as rejection, can create space for understanding rather than distance. You might also explore what makes you feel connected to your own body again outside of sex, whether that is through rest, movement, or simply having time that is not consumed by responsibilities. Desire often returns when there is space, not pressure. You are not alone in this, and it is something that can shift with patience and awareness. Take your time.

How Do Busy Couples Keep the Spark Alive in the Marriage?

There is no universal number that defines a “strong marriage,” even though a lot of advice online tries to reduce intimacy to frequency. What matters more is whether both of you feel connected, desired, and satisfied with the rhythm you have, rather than whether it matches an external benchmark.

When work is demanding and energy is limited, intimacy often fades because it gets deprioritised or squeezed into whatever time is left. Over time, that can make it feel like another task rather than something you look forward to. The solution here is less about increasing frequency and more about protecting your space for intentional connection, whether that includes sex or not. This could mean setting aside time where you are not distracted, staying present with each other in small daily moments, and allowing intimacy to exist flexibly as more than just sexual forms. Some weeks will naturally be quieter. That is okay.

Busy couples tend to keep the spark alive not by doing more, but by staying emotionally engaged with each other in ways that feel genuine and unforced. When emotional closeness is maintained, physical intimacy tends to follow more naturally. It is not about hitting a number. It is about not losing each other in the routine.

How Do I Get Out of the 'Friend Zone'?

May 14, 2026, 20:00 IST

The best way to get out of the ‘friend-zone’ is by accepting the dynamic with grace and dignity and moving on with your unrequited feelings. Her behaviour is already giving you useful information. When someone consistently deflects or dismisses romantic plans while still being open to casual hangouts, it often means they are comfortable with the connection as it is, but not interested in taking it further. That is not a puzzle to solve, nor is it a point to try and change someone’s mind about.
Regardless of what Bollywood tells us, this is a boundary being communicated and it is now up to you to decide if you can still honour the friendship that exists.

The most respectful and clarifying way forward, if you believe things are unclear, is to address it gently and directly, without pressure or persuasion. You could say that you enjoy spending time with her and would be interested in exploring something more, but you also want to understand how she sees it so you don’t misread the situation. This gives her space to respond honestly. If she is not interested, the real decision is whether you are comfortable continuing as friends without holding on to the hope that it will change. Trying to “convert” the dynamic is not the romantic gesture that we think it is, and is most likely going to create an insincere dynamic where you feign interest only under the condition that things eventually become romantic.

Clarity, even if it stings a little, is what actually frees you. To be human is to accept rejection with grace and keep moving forward. And you deserve to enjoy your friendships without pressuring them to be something they are not cut out to be.

How Can Estranged Couples Rebuild a Relationship After Separation for Years?

May 3, 2026, 20:00 IST

It is absolutely possible for estranged couples to reconnect, but it rarely ever looks like picking up exactly where you left off. Too much might have happened in the time apart, both individually and within the relationship, for things to simply return to their previous state. What you are really doing is building something new with someone you already have history with, and that can be both an advantage and a challenge.

The first step is often to approach each other with curiosity rather than expectation or presumption, allowing space to observe and relearn who you both are now, recognising what has changed, and communicating about what you are hoping for moving forward. Small, consistent efforts matter more than grand gestures in this phase. Go on dates and court each other all over again, as you would any other new partner. Build new rituals and habits that make room for the new people that you are now, and rely less on old patterns or behaviours unless you have both been able to confirm that those behaviours and practices still apply and feel good.

Conversations that are not only about the past but also about the present, spending time together in low-pressure settings, and gradually rebuilding emotional safety can create a foundation for connection to grow again. It is also important to acknowledge what led to the separation in the first place, not to dwell on it, but to ensure that those patterns are not repeated. Creating clarity on the initial reasons for separation can help you both heal old wounds and feel more confident in your reasons for reviving this relationship. Falling back in love is less about rediscovering something lost and more about choosing each other again, intentionally, with a clearer understanding of what the relationship needs this time.

How To Stop Money Fights in a Relationship With Different Spending Habits?

Money disagreements often look like practical conflicts on the surface, but they tend to carry deeper emotional meanings underneath. One partner might associate saving with security and control, while the other might associate spending with freedom or reward, and when those values clash, it can feel like you are fundamentally mismatched rather than just having different habits. Over time, these repeated arguments can create a kind of emotional fatigue that spills into other parts of the relationship, including intimacy, because it becomes harder to feel close when you are constantly negotiating or defending your choices.

Finding a way out of this does not mean forcing alignment on every decision, but understanding what money represents for each of you and building a system that respects both perspectives. This might look like creating shared financial goals alongside individual spending freedom, or agreeing on certain boundaries that reduce friction without micromanaging each other. The shift happens when the conversation moves from “who is right” to “how do we make this work for both of us.” It is also important to have these discussions outside of moments of conflict, when you are both calmer and more open to listening. Intimacy often returns when tensions are resolved and reduced, because emotional safety and connection begin to feel possible again. You are not just solving for money. You are rebuilding comfort, trust, safety and connection between you.

For some couples, casual flirting or liking photos is harmless and even expected. For others, it starts to feel like a slow leak in emotional exclusivity, especially when the relationship already feels a little stagnant, strained or disconnected.

The more useful question here is not whether this fits the label of cheating, but what it represents for both of you. Sometimes these behaviours are less about wanting someone else and more about seeking novelty, validation, or a sense of aliveness that feels missing in the relationship. Sometimes, we may even resort to it as a bid for attention from our partners, because even a disagreement or a fight about exclusivity and boundaries can feel like being wanted by them. That does not automatically mean something is wrong with your bond, nor that anyone is being ‘toxic’ necessarily, but it does point to something that might need care and recalibration. Instead of turning this into an accusation or a stern rule-setting exercise, it can help to have a conversation about what feels okay, what feels uncomfortable, and why.

You might find that you both have slightly different thresholds or definitions, and aligning on those boundaries can bring clarity to your connection. Attraction outside a relationship can exist. But a lack of clarity and transparency between partners is where things can quickly go awry.

It simply means you want to reconnect with yourself, your thoughts, and your own pace without constant interaction. When this need is ignored, it can sometimes lead to irritability or emotional fatigue, which then affects the relationship in ways that feel confusing because everything else seems “fine.”

The key is how this is communicated. Framing your need for space as something that helps you show up better in the relationship, rather than something that takes away from it, can make a big difference. It reassures your partner that this is not about distance or disconnection, but about balance. Healthy intimacy includes both closeness and autonomy. You are allowed to want both.

It’s hard to find any survivors of abuse who would not feel this distance and disconnect from themselves, as we often dissociate or distance ourselves from the reality of our abuse to cope with the violence and neglect.
